selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: no experiments have been run, so we do not yet know how well any modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion performs. 2. What this tests: the simplest configuration, RNA-only with a single profile and the PCA (2000-dimension) RNA encoder, which sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later changes can be compared against one at a time. Planned comparisons are a different RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), image-only, multiprofile pooling, and multimodal fusion. 3. Why now: under a 10-experiment budget, a clear simple anchor lets later results show whether added complexity actually helps, rather than assuming multimodal or multiprofile models win.

1) The only evidence so far is a single RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (val acc 0.485, F1 0.464). We know nothing yet about the image modality, which is the largest unexplored dimension and gates half of the search space, including every multimodal configuration. 2) config_010 (image-only, single-profile, resnet50) gives a matched single-profile baseline for the image modality. Comparing it with config_001 shows whether images carry signal comparable to, weaker than, or stronger than RNA. That result informs whether multimodal fusion is worth pursuing and how much to weight image-heavy configurations. 3) With 8 experiments left, establishing modality-level baselines early reduces the most uncertainty per experiment. Changing only the modality (keeping single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion) isolates its effect cleanly. Encoder, aggregation and profile-setting refinements can then be explored around whichever direction looks stronger.

1) Evidence: RNA-only with PCA (config_001, 0.485 acc / 0.464 F1) is far ahead of image-only with ResNet50 (config_010, 0.208 acc). That makes RNA the dominant modality and the best base to build on. Whether multiprofile aggregation helps is still unknown, and this design axis touches most of the remaining search space. 2) This experiment changes only one thing from config_001: single-profile becomes multiprofile with avgpool, keeping the PCA encoder. Any accuracy change can therefore be attributed to profile setting and aggregation alone. 3) Under a 10-experiment budget, settling the profile-setting question on the strongest modality is the most informative next step. A gain would justify exploring transformer aggregation and other RNA encoders in multiprofile mode. No gain would shift effort toward comparing single-profile RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or multimodal fusion.

1. Evidence: With the pca_n2000 RNA encoder, going from singleprofile to multiprofile avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, with F1 rising alongside it. Image-only resnet50 is weak at 0.208, so RNA multiprofile is the most promising direction. The remaining uncertainties are the aggregation method and the RNA encoder. 2. Test: config_003 changes only the aggregation, avgpool to transformer, holding RNA-only, multiprofile and pca_n2000 fixed. This isolates whether learned set aggregation beats mean pooling. 3. Why now: Aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration, including the multimodal ones, so settling it early makes later choices more efficient. Comparing encoders (scvi or scgpt) in the multiprofile setting is the natural next step, and the 6 remaining experiments leave room for it.

1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only single-profile PCA reached 0.485 accuracy, while image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.208. Multiprofile aggregation with avgpool raised PCA RNA to 0.591 accuracy (F1 0.573), which is the current best. Transformer aggregation did worse at 0.519, so avgpool is the preferred aggregator for now. The RNA encoder choice (PCA vs scVI vs scGPT) is still completely untested, and it is likely a key design choice. 2) Test: config_005 keeps the best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. Any difference in accuracy can therefore be attributed to the representation. 3) Why now: an encoder that beats PCA could lift the best score and would also be the better base for later multimodal or scGPT experiments. Adding the weak image modality now would be a lower-confidence bet, and the encoder question has to be answered before the remaining budget is spent on fusion variants.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool clearly beats singleprofile (0.591 vs 0.485 with PCA) and transformer aggregation (0.519). Switching from PCA to scVI under multiprofile avgpool raised accuracy to the current best (0.650, F1 0.628), so the RNA encoder is an important lever. scGPT is the one RNA encoder not yet tested. Image-only singleprofile is weak (0.208), so adding images is not clearly promising yet. 2. Test: run scGPT in the best-known setting (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool). This changes only the encoder relative to config_005 and config_002, so it directly shows whether scGPT beats scVI. 3. Why now: it could produce a new best and also decides which RNA encoder to carry into the remaining experiments. Those can then test whether weighted or concat fusion with an image encoder adds value on top of the strongest RNA backbone.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool clearly beats singleprofile (0.591 vs 0.485 with PCA). Avgpool also beat transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519). Among RNA encoders, scVI is best (0.650 vs PCA 0.591 and scGPT 0.530). The image-only ResNet50 baseline is weak (0.208), so the open question is whether adding image features to the best RNA pipeline helps or hurts. 2) This experiment keeps the best RNA setup fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 images with weighted fusion. Weighted fusion can learn to down-weight a weak modality, so it is the safest test of whether images add complementary signal. 3) With three experiments left, this changes only one factor (adding a modality) on top of the best setup. A gain would point toward fusion and image-encoder refinements, such as concat fusion or ViT-L. No gain would tell us to put the remaining budget into RNA-only variants such as scVI with transformer aggregation.

1) Evidence: multiprofile avgpool clearly beats singleprofile and transformer aggregation for RNA. scVI is the strongest RNA encoder (0.650). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion (config_031) gave the best result so far (0.678 acc, 0.646 F1), even though ResNet50 alone was weak (0.208). The image encoder is the main untested choice: ImageNet ViT-L has not been tried in any setting. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. That isolates whether stronger image features add more to the multimodal model. 3) The image branch looks like the weakest part of the current best model, so improving it is likely to give a larger gain than changing fusion type (concat vs weighted). Exploiting the strong scVI + avgpool + weighted base keeps risk low. The result will also guide the final experiment, either a fusion comparison or keeping this image encoder.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy. It beat the matching ResNet50 run (0.678), and multimodal runs beat the best RNA-only run (0.650). Across the RNA-only runs, avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519 for PCA). scVI was the best RNA encoder. The fusion method, however, has never been varied: every multimodal run used weighted fusion. 2. Test: config_036 keeps everything from the best configuration and changes only the fusion, from weighted to concat. This isolates the one untested design choice that could still raise accuracy. 3. Why now: With two experiments left, the better choice is to improve the strongest configuration through a single untested factor. The alternatives are weaker: transformer aggregation already looked worse, and scGPT and PCA were weaker RNA encoders. The result also sets up the last experiment. If concat wins, the final run can test a related variant. If it loses, weighted fusion is supported, and the last run can try something else, such as transformer aggregation.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. ViT-L beat ResNet50, and concat slightly beat weighted fusion with the other choices held fixed. Aggregation is the main open question: transformer aggregation was tested only once, with RNA-only PCA, where it trailed avgpool (0.519 vs 0.591). It has never been tested with the stronger scVI encoder or with multimodal inputs, where richer per-profile features might benefit from learned aggregation. 2) This run keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation. That isolates whether learned aggregation helps in the strongest setting. 3) Only the best accuracy counts and this is the final run, so I want an option with a real chance of beating 0.715. Swapping ViT-L for ResNet50 (config_030) would likely score lower, since ResNet50 trailed ViT-L under weighted fusion. Single-profile variants have been consistently weaker. That leaves the aggregation change as the most plausible remaining way to improve on the current best.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known yet about which modality, RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion helps. The principles also warn against assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models will beat simpler ones. 2. What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-variance setup. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be measured against. Each later run can then change one factor at a time, such as the encoder (scVI or scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, adding images, or the fusion method, so its effect can be isolated. 3. Why it is the best use of the first slot: with 10 experiments, a clean baseline makes every later comparison easier to read. Starting with a complex multimodal model would mix several design choices together, so any result would be hard to attribute to a specific factor.

1) Evidence: the only result so far is an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. Nothing is known yet about the image modality, which is a major branch of the search space (half of the multimodal configurations depend on the image encoder). 2) This experiment tests an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model (config_010). It keeps the profile setting the same as the baseline, adds no aggregation or fusion, and changes only the modality, so it isolates RNA versus image as a feature source. 3) It is the best use of the next experiment because the modality question has the largest effect on where the remaining 8 experiments should go. If images are competitive or better, the search should move toward image or multimodal configurations. If they are much worse, the search can focus on improving the RNA encoder and testing multiprofile aggregation. One clean comparison now gives the most information for directing the rest of the budget.

1. Evidence: RNA-only PCA singleprofile (acc 0.485, F1 0.464) far outperforms ResNet50 image-only singleprofile (acc 0.208, F1 0.172). RNA is clearly the stronger modality, but we don't yet know whether profile setting, RNA encoder or fusion matters most. 2. Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation, while keeping the best-known RNA-only PCA setup. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles improves accuracy. 3. Why now: multiprofile aggregation applies across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal configurations, so the answer will guide many later choices. Using avgpool first gives a clean, low-complexity baseline before trying transformer aggregation, other RNA encoders, or fusion with the weak image modality.

1) Evidence: RNA is clearly the stronger modality (0.485 RNA vs. 0.208 image in the single-profile setting). Switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy, with F1 rising alongside). This makes RNA multiprofile the most promising direction. The open question is whether a learned aggregator can extract more from multiple profiles than simple averaging. 2) config_003 keeps everything else fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer, so any difference can be attributed to aggregation. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the strongest result so far with a clean single-variable comparison. Aggregation needs only one experiment to resolve, whereas the encoder question (scvi_n200, scgpt) needs two. Settling aggregation first leaves budget to test the encoders under the better aggregator, and later fusion with images if warranted.

1. Evidence: RNA is clearly the stronger modality. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.208 accuracy, against 0.485 for RNA-only. Multiprofile avgpool gave the largest gain so far (0.591 accuracy, F1 0.573), beating singleprofile and transformer aggregation. All RNA results so far use the PCA encoder, so the RNA encoder is the main untested design choice. 2. Test: keep the best setup (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swap PCA for scGPT embeddings. This isolates the effect of a foundation-model RNA representation. 3. Why now: with 5 experiments left, finding the best RNA encoder in the top setting matters more than testing image fusion yet, since the image signal is weak. If scGPT beats PCA, it becomes the base for later multimodal tests. If not, scVI (config_005) or adding images to PCA avgpool (config_018/019) are the next steps.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA, avgpool) at 0.591 accuracy and 0.573 F1. On the RNA side, multiprofile beat singleprofile, avgpool beat transformer, and PCA beat scGPT. Multimodal fusion is the largest untested design dimension. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208), so it is unclear whether images add complementary signal or just noise. 2. Test: config_019 adds ResNet50 image features to the best RNA setup and changes nothing else, so it isolates whether adding images helps. Weighted fusion is the lower-risk choice because it can down-weight a weak image branch, which plain concatenation cannot. 3. Why now: the multimodal question has a large potential upside and governs most of the remaining search space. With 4 experiments left, settling it now leaves room to try the scVI encoder (config_005) or the ViT-L image encoder afterwards, depending on the result.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1. That is about 4.8 points above the matching RNA-only setup (config_002, 0.591), so the image modality adds signal even though ResNet50 alone is weak (0.208). The image encoder choice is still unexplored: ImageNet ViT-L has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps everything in config_019 fixed and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. It shows whether a stronger image representation adds more to the fused model. 3) This is the best use of a limited budget because the image branch looks like the weakest part of the current best model, so it has the most room to improve. Changing one factor gives a clean comparison. The remaining runs can then test fusion type (concat) or the scVI RNA encoder on whichever image encoder wins.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (multimodal, pca_n2000 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.639, F1 0.620). Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l gave nearly the same result (0.635), so the image encoder seems to matter little. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation for RNA (0.591 vs 0.519). pca_n2000 beat scgpt (0.591 vs 0.530). Fusion type has not been tested at all; every multimodal run used weighted fusion. 2. Test: config_018 is identical to the best configuration except that it uses concat fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion strategy cleanly. 3. Why now: Fusion is a core multimodal design choice with no evidence yet, and this one-variable change to the top configuration could directly improve the best score. The two remaining experiments can then go to the untested scvi_n200 RNA encoder, combined with whichever fusion type wins.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_019 (PCA + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.639 accuracy. Weighted fusion beat concat (0.639 vs 0.619), and the two image encoders were nearly tied (0.639 vs 0.635). Avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519), and PCA beat scGPT (0.591 vs 0.530). The RNA representation is the strongest driver of performance, yet the scVI encoder has never been tested. 2. Test: This keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI, isolating whether scVI improves the dominant modality. 3. Why now: With 2 experiments left, this single-variable change to the best setup is the most plausible way to beat 0.639 and settles the main open design question. If it helps, the last experiment can pair scVI with ViT-L. If not, we keep the PCA-based best.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_031 (scVI + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion; acc 0.678, F1 0.646). Swapping PCA for scVI gave a clear gain over config_019 (0.639). Weighted fusion beat concat (0.639 vs 0.619), and avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the RNA-only setting (0.591 vs 0.519). With PCA, ViT-L and ResNet50 performed about the same (0.635 vs 0.639), so which image encoder works best with scVI is still uncertain. 2) This run changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) and keeps the strongest recipe: scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion. It tests whether ViT-L image features combine better with scVI embeddings. 3) This is the last experiment, so exploitation matters most. A single-factor variant of the current best has a realistic chance of beating it. The alternatives look weaker: concat fusion and transformer aggregation both underperformed in earlier runs, and the scGPT variants have been weaker than PCA and scVI.

What this tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-variance configuration. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against one design choice at a time: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), image-only models, profile setting and aggregation, and multimodal fusion. 3. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001), with accuracy 0.485 and F1 0.464. We know nothing yet about the image modality, which appears in more than two-thirds of the remaining configurations. 2. 1. Evidence: RNA-only PCA single-profile (0.485 acc, 0.464 F1) clearly beats image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.208 acc, 0.172 F1). RNA looks like the stronger signal, but this rests on one run per modality. 2. Test: config_002 keeps the RNA-only PCA setup and changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps, and simple averaging is the lower-risk first check before trying the transformer. 3. Why now: profile setting applies across nearly every remaining configuration (RNA, image and multimodal), so learning its effect early guides much of the remaining budget. Building on the strongest baseline also gives a good chance of improving the best accuracy. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and fusion with the weak image branch can be tested once the profile question is clearer.

1. Evidence: RNA is clearly the stronger modality (0.485 accuracy for RNA-only versus 0.208 for image-only, single-profile). Moving RNA from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy to 0.591 and F1 to 0.573, so multiprofile RNA is the most promising direction. The main open question is whether the aggregation method or the RNA encoder drives further gains. 2. This experiment keeps the best setting fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only aggregation from avgpool to transformer. That isolates whether a learned set aggregator beats mean pooling. 3. Aggregation is shared across every multiprofile setup, both RNA-only and multimodal, so this answer will guide many later choices. The remaining six experiments can then compare RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) under the better aggregator, and test multimodal fusion only after the strongest RNA backbone is identified.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, pca_n2000 with avgpool (0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1). It clearly beats the single-profile PCA run (0.485) and the transformer aggregation run (0.519). Image-only ResNet50 is very weak (0.208), so the RNA side is carrying performance. The main untested question is which RNA encoder works best: only PCA has been tried. 2. This experiment keeps the best profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder from PCA to scVI (n200). That isolates the effect of the RNA representation. 3. Rationale: RNA encoder choice likely sets the ceiling for both the RNA-only and the multimodal configurations, so settling it now helps every later choice. Changing one variable from the current best is a cleaner test than jumping to multimodal fusion, especially given how weak the image signal looks. scVI was chosen over scGPT as a well-established embedding for cell-state tasks. scGPT can be tested next if scVI does not improve on PCA.

1. Evidence: RNA is far stronger than image so far (0.48 vs 0.21 single-profile). Multiprofile avgpool beat single-profile and transformer aggregation with PCA (0.59 vs 0.48 and 0.52). Switching from PCA to scVI under multiprofile avgpool raised accuracy to the current best of 0.650 (F1 0.628). The main open question is the third RNA encoder, scGPT, which has never been tested. 2. This experiment keeps the best-performing setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. That isolates whether a foundation-model embedding beats scVI. 3. The encoder has been the most influential choice so far, so testing scGPT is the most informative single step. Its result tells us which RNA encoder to use in the remaining runs. Those can then test whether adding image features through fusion (e.g., avgpool with concat or weighted) improves on the best RNA-only result, rather than assuming multimodal helps.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_005 (RNA-only, multiprofile, scVI, avgpool) at 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Multiprofile with avgpool has consistently beaten single-profile and transformer aggregation, and scVI has beaten PCA and scGPT. The largest open question is whether adding the image modality helps. ResNet50 image-only was weak (0.208), so it is unclear whether images add complementary signal or just noise. 2. Test: This experiment keeps the best RNA setup fixed (scVI, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion. Weighted fusion should be able to down-weight a weak modality, which makes it the safer way to measure whether images add anything. Because only the modality changes relative to config_005, the comparison isolates the effect of fusion. 3. Why now: This both exploits the strongest configuration and resolves the most important remaining design choice, RNA-only versus multimodal. With 3 experiments left after this one, the result will tell me whether to spend the rest of the budget on fusion variants (concat, ViT-L) or on refining RNA-only settings.

1. Evidence: Multiprofile avgpool clearly beats singleprofile (0.591 vs 0.485 with PCA) and beats transformer aggregation (0.519). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested (0.650). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion gave the best result so far (config_031: 0.678 accuracy, 0.646 F1). That gain is modest, and ResNet50 on its own is weak (0.208), so the quality of the image representation is a key open question. ImageNet ViT-L has not been tested in any setting. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L. That isolates whether a stronger image representation adds more to the scVI multimodal model. 3. With 2 experiments left, the image encoder is the untested choice most likely to shift accuracy by a meaningful amount. A fusion swap (concat) is a smaller, more incremental change that can still be tested in the final experiment on whichever image encoder wins.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the RNA-only comparison (0.591 vs 0.519). scVI is the strongest RNA encoder tested, and ViT-L beat ResNet50 under multimodal fusion. Fusion type is the only major design choice not yet tested: every multimodal run has used weighted fusion. 2. Test: config_036 keeps the leading setup fixed and changes only the fusion method from weighted to concat. This isolates whether the fusion method matters. 3. Why now: the evidence does not favor the transformer variant, and the other options are weaker. Changing the one untested factor on the best configuration is the cleanest experiment with a real chance of beating 0.706. It also tells the final experiment which fusion to keep.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_036 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile avgpool, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Each component has beaten its alternative: scVI beat PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beat ResNet50, multiprofile beat singleprofile, and concat edged out weighted fusion. The main untested choice in this strong multimodal setting is aggregation. The only transformer data point is a single RNA-only PCA run, where transformer aggregation did worse than avgpool. That is weak evidence for the multimodal case, because richer scVI + ViT-L features may benefit from learned attention across profiles. 2) Test: keep every best-known choice fixed and swap avgpool for transformer aggregation. This isolates the aggregation effect in the top configuration. 3) Rationale: with only one experiment left, the goal is the best chance of beating 0.715. The other options look unlikely to win. ResNet50 with concat (config_030) sits on the weaker image encoder. Swapping in scGPT or PCA moves to clearly weaker RNA encoders. Singleprofile variants drop the profile setting that consistently helped. This is the only remaining one-change extension of the best configuration with a realistic chance of a higher score.

1. Evidence: multiprofile avgpool clearly beats singleprofile and transformer aggregation (RNA-only: 0.591 vs 0.485 and 0.519). Adding images helps further.
